lead: A crane, a bicycle frame, a rice sack on a rope — each is a real body with an awkward shape that bends under load. Mechanics cannot solve that directly, so it swaps the body for an ideal model: a particle, or a rigid body. Newton's three laws then act on the model, in consistent SI units, and the answer comes out as a force with a magnitude and a direction. This chapter builds that chain — model, law, unit — because every later problem in statics and dynamics stands on it.

sections.h3: The subject, and the models it uses

blocks.text: Engineering mechanics studies bodies at rest or in motion under forces. Statics deals with bodies at rest. Dynamics deals with bodies in motion, and splits again: kinematics is the geometry of motion — how position, velocity and acceleration change with time, without asking what causes them — and kinetics is the study of the forces that cause that motion (see Unit 5, Kinematics and Kinetics of Particles).
Three idealizations do most of the work.

items: Particle: all the mass sits at one point, so size is ignored. Fair when the body is small compared with the distances involved, or when rotation does not matter.
Rigid body: the distance between any two of its points never changes. Deformation is handed to a later subject.
Continuum: matter is spread smoothly, so density can be defined at a point.

blocks.text: The fundamental quantities are length, mass and time. Force is built from them, as the next section shows.

sections.h3: Newton's laws, weight, and line of action

blocks.text: First law. A body stays at rest, or moves with constant velocity in a straight line, unless a net external force acts on it. This defines force as whatever changes motion, and it is the parent of equilibrium: zero net force means no change of velocity (see 1.6).

Second law. The net force equals the rate of change of momentum. For constant mass, F = ma: F is the net force in newtons (N), m the mass in kilograms (kg), a the acceleration in metres per second squared (m/s²).
Third law. If A pushes B, B pushes A with an equal and opposite force. The pair acts on two different bodies, so both never appear on one free body diagram (see 1.5).

blocks.where: W is weight in N; m is mass in kg; g is the acceleration due to gravity, 9.81 m/s² near Earth's surface. It comes from Newton's gravitation law F = G m₁m₂/r², with G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², by putting m₁ = Earth's mass and r = Earth's radius.

blocks.text: Mass is a property of the body, the same on the Moon. Weight is a force, and changes with g. The line of action of a force is the straight line along which it acts; for a rigid body, sliding a force along its own line of action changes nothing (Unit 2).

sections.h3: Units, the kgf, and the homogeneity check

blocks.text: SI has seven base units; mechanics needs three — the metre (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, the second (s) for time. Force is derived: 1 newton gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s², so 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². A 100 g apple weighs roughly 1 N.

Prefixes scale these: k = 10³, M = 10⁶, m = 10⁻³, µ = 10⁻⁶. So 1 kN = 1000 N. The kilogram-force (kgf) is the weight of a 1 kg mass under standard gravity: 1 kgf = 9.81 N. Tyre gauges and older drawings still use it. Convert before substituting, and never add kgf to N inside one equation.

Every equation derived from physical laws is homogeneous: each term carries the same units. Empirical formulas fitted to data are the exception — their constants carry units so the terms still match. Test v² = u² + 2as. The left side is (m/s)² = m²/s²; u² is m²/s²; and 2as is m/s² × m = m²/s². All three agree, so the equation passes. The number 2 has no units. A mismatch means either the formula is misremembered or a conversion was missed — a ten-second check that catches most unit errors.

examples.question: A 25 kg sack of rice hangs from a single rope. Take g = 9.81 m/s². (a) Find the weight of the sack in N and in kgf. (b) The rope is rated for 300 N — is it safe? (c) Check whether v² = u² + 2as is homogeneous in SI units.
steps: (a) Weight is mass times g: W = m g = 25 kg × 9.81 m/s² = 245.25 N.
Convert to kgf by dividing by 9.81 N/kgf: 245.25 N ÷ 9.81 N/kgf = 25 kgf. This is expected: the weight of a 25 kg mass is 25 kgf by definition under standard gravity.
(b) Compare with the rating: 245.25 N < 300 N, so the rope is safe. The margin is 300 − 245.25 = 54.75 N.

(c) Units of each term of v² = u² + 2as: [v²] = m²/s²; [u²] = m²/s²; [2as] = (m/s²)(m) = m²/s². All three terms agree, so the equation is homogeneous. The constant 2 is dimensionless and does not affect the check.
examples.answer: The weight is 245.25 N, that is 25 kgf; the rope is safe because 245.25 N is less than its 300 N rating, with 54.75 N to spare; and v² = u² + 2as is homogeneous, since every term has units m²/s².
examples.check:
m = 25
g = 9.81  # m/s^2
n_per_kgf = 9.81
rating = 300.0
W = m * g
kgf = W / n_per_kgf
print(round(W, 2))
print(round(kgf, 2))
print(round(rating - W, 2))

traps: Reporting 25 kg as the weight. Mass is in kg, weight is a force in N; the weight here is 245.25 N.
Mixing kgf and N in one equation. Convert everything to N first, or write kgf throughout, never both.
Using g = 10 m/s² when the paper says 9.81, or the reverse. Use the g the question gives.
Drawing action and reaction on the same free body diagram and cancelling them. They act on two different bodies.
Treating a body as a particle when its size decides the answer — a ladder against a wall cannot topple if it is a point.

quiz.q: Define a particle and a rigid body as used in mechanics.
quiz.a: A particle is a body whose mass is taken to be concentrated at a single point, so its size is ignored. A rigid body is a body in which the distance between any two points stays constant under load, so it does not deform.

quiz.q: State the SI unit of force and define it.
quiz.a: The newton (N). One newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s², so 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².

quiz.q: Why does mechanics replace a real machine part by an ideal model before solving?
quiz.a: A real part has an awkward shape and deforms, so its equations are far too hard to solve by hand. The ideal model keeps only what decides the answer — for example mass and position for a particle — so Newton's laws give a usable result. The engineer then judges whether the simplification was acceptable.

quiz.q: Distinguish kinematics from kinetics, with one example each.
quiz.a: Kinematics describes the geometry of motion — position, velocity and acceleration against time — without asking what causes it; for a projectile, it gives those quantities at each instant of flight. Kinetics relates motion to the forces that cause it; for the same projectile, it explains that motion through the force of gravity.

quiz.q: An 80 kg person stands on a weighing machine. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find the weight in N and in kgf.
quiz.a: W = m g = 80 × 9.81 = 784.8 N. In kgf: 784.8 ÷ 9.81 = 80 kgf. The reading is 784.8 N, which is 80 kgf.

quiz.q: Check whether s = ut + ½at² is homogeneous in SI units.
quiz.a: [s] = m. [ut] = (m/s)(s) = m. [½at²] = (m/s²)(s²) = m. All three terms are metres, so the equation is homogeneous; the factors ½ and the squares carry no units of their own.

quiz.q: A student says the reaction to the weight of a hanging sack is the tension in the rope. Is this correct?
quiz.a: No. By the third law the partner of Earth pulling the sack down is the sack pulling Earth up, with equal magnitude. Tension is a separate contact force from the rope. The sack hangs in equilibrium because tension balances weight, but that is a balance of two different forces on one body, not an action–reaction pair.

quiz.q: A ladder leans against a wall. Explain why the particle model fails here and which idealization you must use.
quiz.a: A particle has no size and no orientation, so it has no point of contact with the wall or the floor and no lever arm. It cannot tip, slide, or feel a moment. The ladder's behaviour depends on where the forces act along its length, so it must be treated as a rigid body, with geometry and moments included (Unit 2, and ladder friction in Unit 3).

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice the same chain — idealize, apply the law, check the units — is what simulation software automates: finite element codes keep the deformation that the rigid body model throws away, and CFD codes keep the continuum. The value of g itself is not constant; it falls with altitude and varies slightly with latitude, which matters for satellite and missile work.
